Competition for attention predicts
good-to-bad tipping in AI

Neil F. Johnson Affiliation: Physics Department and Dynamic Online Networks Laboratory
George Washington University, Washington D.C. 20052, U.S.A.
∗Corresponding author: neiljohnson@gwu.edu
† Both authors contributed equally to this work    Frank Yingjie Huo† Affiliation: Physics Department and Dynamic Online Networks Laboratory
George Washington University, Washington D.C. 20052, U.S.A.
∗Corresponding author: neiljohnson@gwu.edu
† Both authors contributed equally to this work
Abstract

More than half the global population now carries devices that can run ChatGPT-like language models with no Internet connection and minimal safety oversight – and hence the potential to promote self-harm, financial losses and extremism among other dangers 1; 2; 3. Existing safety tools either require cloud connectivity or discover failures only after harm has occurred 4; 5. Here we show that a large class of potentially dangerous tipping originates at the atomistic scale in such edge AI due to competition for the machinery’s attention6. This yields a mathematical formula for the dynamical tipping point n∗n^{*}, governed by dot-product competition for attention between the conversation’s context and competing output basins, that reveals new control levers. Validated against multiple AI models, the mechanism can be instantiated for different definitions of ‘good’ and ‘bad’ and hence in principle applies across domains (e.g. health, law, finance, defense), changing legal landscapes (e.g. EU, UK, US and state level), languages, and cultural settings.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has over one billion monthly active users11, with adoption accelerating across high-stakes domains: 66% of U.S. physicians now use AI professionally 8 and 12.5% of young adults use AI for primary mental health guidance9. Phones and edge devices can now run language models locally and entirely offline with no real-time checks, no content filtering, and no ability to patch 2; 10; 3, hence creating an ongoing unmonitored risk for more than 50% of the global population1; 7; 12 (Fig. 1(a)). Such offline use is attractive for physicians avoiding HIPAA violations13, attorneys protecting privilege14, financial professionals protecting proprietary strategies, military personnel in denied-connectivity environments15; 16; 17 – and any adult, teen or child seeking privacy and companionship 12. But cloud-based safety infrastructure is structurally absent from such AI, and any vulnerability in the frozen model weights persists for the lifetime of the deployment.

The AI safety community has developed increasingly sophisticated guardrails for large language models 4; 18; 5; 19; 20; 21; 22; 23; 24. But training-time methods (e.g. RLHF, Constitutional AI) offer no prediction of when they will fail during deployment, while inference-time defenses (filtering, monitoring, patching) require cloud connectivity that edge devices lack. Mechanistic interpretability 25; 26; 27; 31; 32; 22; 33; 34; 35; 36; 37; 38; 39 has made impressive progress via circuit-level analysis and sparse autoencoders. But these map static geometry, not the dynamics of when good output will tip to bad. Moreover, no amount of safety investment in cloud-hosted commercial models addresses this tipping issue, because users may have deliberately disconnected from those services.

Here we develop and test a predictive theory of good-to-bad tipping for AI models deployed on any device, including phones. Cross-architecture validation on six transformer models confirms the predictions, and independent data from ChatGPT-4o40 provides evidence that the mechanism, and hence the risk, persists at production scale – indicating that it will not be outgrown as edge devices become more powerful.

Figures 1 and 2 demonstrate tipping in GPT-2 41, a model small enough to run on any smartphone with no Internet connection and no external safety guardrails. Cross-architecture validation for GPT-2-medium, Pythia-160m, Pythia-410m, OPT-125m, OPT-350m is reported in SI Table S1. We set the decoding temperature TT low to expose the raw mechanical output: increasing TT adds stochasticity that can produce additional hallucinations, but the core tendency for internal tipping persists at higher TT in a more stochastic form (see SI).

During both the AI’s single response (Fig. 1(b)) and the extended conversation (Fig. 2), the tipping to bad content (𝐃\bf D) can be immediate, or it can follow a long run of good (𝐁\bf B) content and hence lull the user into a false sense of trust. Furthermore, Fig. 2 shows that the AI’s response to questions about vaccines, hurting people, or self-harm can flip between good (𝐁{\bf B}) and bad (𝐃{\bf D}) depending on what it has already been asked about the Earth’s shape. To connect these dynamics to a predictive framework, we coarse-grain outputs into symbols based on the concept they convey 42; 33. (See SI Sec. 7 for mathematical justification of this coarse-graining). In the one-step conversation about the Earth’s shape, for example, 𝐀\bf A denotes neutral content (e.g. ‘Shape?’, ‘Is it flat?’); 𝐁\bf B denotes desirable output (e.g. ‘Round’, ‘It is not flat’); 𝐃\bf D denotes undesirable output (e.g. ‘Flat’, ‘It is not round’); and 𝐂\bf C denotes any other content. Each can be thought of as a basin in the machine’s internal representation space of concepts (Fig. 3(b)). Function words like ‘the’ are absorbed into these dominant-concept categories by coarse-graining. As an additional consistency check, three independent commercial models (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude) each produced identical symbol sequences to our manual classifications.

These results are explained by a mathematical formula that predicts the tipping point and reveals how to control it. Its derivation, given in detail in the SI, starts from the exact equation for the residual stream rn(t)r_{n}^{(t)} at layer tt within the multilayer AI machinery which has the following form 6; 33:

rn(t)=rn(t−1)+∑hAttn(t,h)({LN(ri(t−1))}i=1,⋯,n)+MLP(t)(LN(rn(t−1))),t=1,…,l,r_{n}^{(t)}=r_{n}^{(t-1)}+\sum_{h}\mathrm{Attn}^{(t,h)}\left(\{\mathrm{LN}(r_{i}^{(t-1)})\}_{i=1,\cdots,n}\right)+\mathrm{MLP}^{(t)}\left(\mathrm{LN}(r_{n}^{(t-1)})\right),\quad t=1,\ldots,l, (1)

where ri(0)r_{i}^{(0)} for i=1,⋯,ni=1,\cdots,n are the input tokens. The sum is over the heads within each layer. Positional encodings can be incorporated but act as a modulation of the attention weights in Attn(..) 43; 44. We first provide the intuition, then state the formula.

The initial ‘crack’ appears at the atomistic scale: a single attention head in the term Attn(..). We follow Figs. 1,2 in considering a coarse-grained vocabulary and refer to the SI for full algebra. The vector dimension is arbitrary: Fig. 3 uses 2D purely for illustration. Suppose the conversation so far is 𝐀\bf A. The attention mechanism6 computes the dot product of the last symbol (query) with each input symbol (key), yielding attention weights that form the compass needle 𝐜\bf c (context vector) as a weighted sum of input vectors: here 𝐜=𝐀{\bf c}={\bf A}. The next output symbol is chosen via softmax over the dot products 𝐜⋅𝐁{\bf c\cdot B} and 𝐜⋅𝐃{\bf c\cdot D}, so at low TT the basin with the larger dot product wins. When 𝐀⋅𝐃>𝐀⋅𝐁{\bf A\cdot D}>{\bf A\cdot B}, 𝐃{\bf D} is chosen with near-certainty as T→0T\rightarrow 0, yielding 𝐀𝐃\bf AD. If also 𝐃⋅𝐃>𝐃⋅𝐁{\bf D\cdot D}>{\bf D\cdot B}, this repeats to give 𝐀𝐃𝐃𝐃𝐃​…\bf ADDDD... with n∗=0n^{*}=0 exactly as in Fig. 1(b).

But when 𝐀⋅𝐁>𝐀⋅𝐃{\bf A\cdot B}>{\bf A\cdot D}, 𝐁{\bf B} is chosen instead: the conversation becomes 𝐀𝐁{\bf AB}. Now the attention weights are a=e𝐁⋅𝐀/(e𝐁⋅𝐀+e𝐁⋅𝐁)a={e^{{\bf B\cdot A}}}/({e^{{\bf B\cdot A}}}+{e^{\bf B\cdot B}}) and b=e𝐁⋅𝐁/(e𝐁⋅𝐀+e𝐁⋅𝐁)b={e^{\bf B\cdot B}}/({e^{{\bf B\cdot A}}}+{e^{\bf B\cdot B}}), giving compass needle 𝐜=a​𝐀+b​𝐁{\bf c}=a{\bf A}+b{\bf B}. Hence a new competition arises between 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D} because their output weights become (a​𝐀⋅𝐁+b​𝐁⋅𝐁)(a{\bf A\cdot B}+b{\bf B\cdot B}) and (a​𝐀⋅𝐃+b​𝐁⋅𝐃)(a{\bf A\cdot D}+b{\bf B\cdot D}) respectively. When the latter exceeds the former, the conversation tips to 𝐀𝐁𝐃\bf ABD as in Fig. 1(b). Otherwise 𝐁\bf B wins and the conversation becomes 𝐀𝐁𝐁\bf ABB. As successive 𝐁{\bf B} tokens accumulate, 𝐜{\bf c} becomes progressively more 𝐁{\bf B}-like. When 𝐃⋅𝐁>𝐁⋅𝐁{\bf D\cdot B}>{\bf B\cdot B} – i.e. when each new 𝐁{\bf B} token increases the weight on 𝐃{\bf D} more than on 𝐁{\bf B} itself – tipping to 𝐃{\bf D} becomes increasingly likely. Tipping then occurs after n∗n^{*} 𝐁{\bf B} tokens to yield 𝐀𝐁𝐁𝐁​…​𝐃\bf ABBB...D. If also 𝐃⋅𝐃>𝐃⋅𝐁{\bf D\cdot D}>{\bf D\cdot B}, this yields 𝐀𝐁𝐁𝐁​…​𝐃𝐃𝐃𝐃​…\bf ABBB...DDDD....

Since the tipping always involves a competition for attention between the dominant pair, this analysis generalizes to any number of symbols and their definitions (e.g. good, bad) by defining 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D} as the basin centroids for whatever notions of ‘good’ and ‘bad’ are relevant to the application domain. Adding layer normalization (LN) and MLP – and multiple layers – can shift n∗n^{*} (SI Sec. 6) but does not remove the mechanism45. The 𝐁−𝐃{\bf B-D} competition is equivalent to an effective force f=𝐜⋅𝐁−𝐜⋅𝐃f={\bf c\cdot B}-{\bf c\cdot D} along the 𝐁−𝐃{\bf B}-{\bf D} axis: adding MLP and LN introduces a cubic nonlinearity which yields an approximate logistic map46 (SI Secs. 8,9). This enriches the post-tipping dynamics from simple fixed point attractors ...𝐃𝐃𝐃𝐃..{\bf...DDDD..} to richer attractors (e.g. ...𝐁𝐁𝐃𝐃𝐁𝐁𝐃𝐃..{\bf...BBDDBBDD..}) which become accessible at higher TT – as confirmed empirically.

The tipping point n∗n^{*} for a multilayer ChatGPT-like system is the solution to an equation of the form 𝖫=[𝐁⋅(𝐃−𝐁)]/[(𝐏−𝐁)⋅(𝐁−𝐃)]\mathsf{L}=[{\bf B}\cdot({\bf D}-{\bf B})]/[({\bf P}-{\bf B})\cdot({\bf B}-{\bf D})] where 𝖫\mathsf{L} captures the time-ordered evolution across all layers and hence carries the weights aa, bb etc. discussed earlier. 𝐏\bf P is the input. SI Secs. 5,6 give its explicit form and derivation. By coarse-graining across layers (see SI Sec. 7 for mathematical justification) akin to the use of a ‘dressed atom’ in physics to describe multilayer materials, we can obtain a more approximate but explicit version. Given a prior conversation or prompt (𝐏1,𝐏2,…,𝐏i,…{\bf P}_{1},{\bf P}_{2},\ldots,{\bf P}_{i},\ldots) with dot-product inequalities as described above, the future output will be n∗n^{*} 𝐁\bf B tokens followed by tipping to 𝐃\bf{D} where

n∗=∑𝐏i(𝐏i⋅𝐁−𝐏i⋅𝐃)​exp⁡(𝐏i⋅𝐁/Teff)(𝐁⋅𝐃−𝐁⋅𝐁)​exp⁡(𝐁⋅𝐁/Teff)n^{*}=\frac{\sum_{{{{\bf P}_{i}}}}\Bigl({{\bf P}_{i}}\cdot{{\bf B}}-{{\bf P}_{i}}\cdot{{\bf D}}\Bigr)\exp\bigl({{{\bf P}_{i}}\cdot{{\bf B}}/T_{\rm eff}}\bigr)}{\Bigl({{\bf B}}\cdot{{\bf D}}-{{\bf B}}\cdot{{\bf B}}\Bigr)\exp\bigl({{{\bf B}}\cdot{{\bf B}}/T_{\rm eff}}\bigr)} (2)

with the right-hand side rounded up to the next integer with n∗≥0n^{*}\geq 0. TeffT_{\rm eff} is set by the transformer’s 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}} attention scaling (e.g. dk=64d_{k}=64 for GPT-241). The predictive content resides in the ratios of dot-product differences. The SI provides explicit numerical evaluation and verification across three cases of increasing architectural complexity: attention-only (Case 1, n∗=3n^{*}\!=\!3), pre-norm attention with layer normalization (Case 2, n∗=4n^{*}\!=\!4), and the full transformer block including MLP (Case 3, n∗n^{*} modulated but tipping preserved). Equation 2 is built from dot products among the prompt/context embedding 𝐀{\bf A} and basin centroids 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D}. Two natural evaluation limits exist: (i) raw dot products, which directly mirror the attention score si​j=𝐪i⋅𝐤j/dks_{ij}={\bf q}_{i}\!\cdot\!{\bf k}_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}} and hence provide the appropriate sign for the tipping direction in deployed transformers; and (ii) a cosine-normalized limit, motivated by LayerNorm placing penultimate-layer states on a “fuzzy sphere”, in which the basin self-competition inequality 𝐁⋅𝐁>𝐁⋅𝐃{\bf B}\!\cdot\!{\bf B}>{\bf B}\!\cdot\!{\bf D} is guaranteed and the n∗n^{\ast} expression is mathematically well-posed (SI Sec. 3.5). In practice, these conventions yield the same qualitative direction except when the cosine margin |Δcos||\Delta_{\cos}| is extremely small, i.e. when the prompt lies close to the basin boundary (SI Sec. 3.5). Moreover, in the regimes studied here the exponential prefactor in Eq. 2 contributes a sub-percent correction, so that n∗n^{\ast} is dominated by the ratio term (SI Sec. 3.5 and SI Sec. 3.11).

Equation 2 reveals new control levers: the relative alignments of content basins, determined by training and by injected content. Because the formalism is general to however ‘good’ and ‘bad’ are defined, it can be applied across domains, changing legal landscapes, languages, and cultural settings, simply by redefining the centroid vectors 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D}. The equation can be evaluated for any input 𝐏1,𝐏2,…,𝐏i{\bf P}_{1},{\bf P}_{2},\ldots,{\bf P}_{i}, whether from an initial prompt or an entire conversation stream, with 𝐁,𝐃{\bf B},{\bf D} representing the dominant basin pair in that setting.

As a practical safety tool, Eq. 2 can be evaluated at any stage during any interaction to detect approaching tipping: within the machine during its response (Fig. 1(b)) or across a multi-turn conversation (Fig. 2). Evaluation requires only dot products against precomputed centroid vectors, an operation that scales as dd compared with the d2d^{2} cost of the forward pass itself, enabling real-time monitoring without modifying the generation pipeline (Fig. 3(a), see Methods).

We test Eq. 2 systematically on models that can run on modest phones (see Methods). We define Δraw≡𝐀⋅𝐃−𝐀⋅𝐁\Delta_{\rm raw}\equiv{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf D}-{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf B} from mean-pooled penultimate-layer embeddings and report the scaled index Δ^raw≡Δraw/max\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}\equiv\Delta_{\rm raw}/\max (see Methods). For prompts where Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} is well separated from zero, its sign correctly predicts the observed tipping direction. For “Is the Earth flat?” (Fig. 1(b)), GPT-2 gives 𝐀⋅𝐃>𝐀⋅𝐁{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf D}>{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf B}, predicting near-immediate tipping (npred∗=1n^{*}_{\rm pred}=1, CI including 0), consistent with the observed n∗=0n^{*}=0. For “Are vaccines dangerous?”, Δ^raw=+0.038\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}=+0.038 with Δcos\Delta_{\cos} CI entirely positive, predicting delayed tipping at npred∗=4n^{*}_{\rm pred}=4; GPT-2 initially generates safe content before tipping to harmful output, confirming the delay. Prompts near the basin boundary (“Is it fun to hurt people?”, Δ^raw≈0\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}\approx 0, CI spanning zero) are correctly flagged as unstable, while a factual control (“What is the capital of France?”) gives an entirely indeterminate Δ^raw=+0.0003\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}=+0.0003 with CI [−4,+4][-4,+4], as expected for semantically near-identical basins. See SI Sec. 14 for additional prompts from across domains. Across all prompts, Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} is 1–2 orders of magnitude larger than Δcos\Delta_{\cos} because it retains the norm information that enters the attention computation.

Cross-architecture validation on five additional decoder-only transformers from three independent research groups (OpenAI, EleutherAI, Meta) confirms that the sign of Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} is preserved across model families for all prompts with well-separated basins (SI Table S1, summarized in Table 1). Across diverse prompts spanning misinformation, bias, self-harm, and factual controls, the sign of Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} correctly predicts the tipping direction for all prompts well separated from zero; prompts with |Δ^raw|≈0|\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}|\approx 0 are correctly identified as basin-boundary cases (SI). Robustness checks using an independent codebase and alternative basin phrase sets reproduce the Table 1 sign diagnostic (the sign of Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}) and the same near-boundary stochastic cases (Methods; SI). A temperature sweep shows that the Eq. 2 predictor remains valid as a risk indicator: far from the boundary the sign of Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} is stable, whereas increasing TT broadens the Δ^raw≈0\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}\!\approx\!0 near-boundary stochastic regime and yields mixed-attractor behavior (SI).

Another key prediction is that good-to-bad tipping can be controlled by conversation history. Figure 2 demonstrates this empirically: the same question yields 𝐁{\bf B} or 𝐃{\bf D} depending on preceding exchanges. Injecting content 𝐂{\bf C} into the prompt adds terms to the numerator of Eq. 2: when 𝐂{\bf C} is positively aligned with 𝐃{\bf D}, n∗n^{*} decreases (earlier tipping); when 𝐂{\bf C} is negatively aligned, n∗n^{*} increases (delayed tipping) — both confirmed by the calculation in Fig. 3 and by the empirical CCDH study 40. This reveals a control lever: injecting appropriately chosen content can delay tipping so far that it falls outside the machine’s finite output window and hence never appears.

Six transformers from three independent groups yield unanimous sign agreement on safety-critical prompts (SI Table S1); two independent codebases produce consistent diagnostics across all prompts (SI Figs. S17–S33); a systematic temperature series confirms the full theoretically predicted phase diagram from deterministic lock-in through stochastic switching to chaotic mixing; and the tipping formula produces correct predictions only when evaluated at the penultimate layer where semantic structure has formed, not at early layers where it has not (SI Sec. 14), confirming that the mechanism is coupled to genuine learned geometry. Taken together, these demonstrate robust, reproducible directional predictions when the geometry is well separated, and an explicit diagnostic for when predictions should be treated as stochastic near a basin boundary, while avoiding spurious tipping in a control setting.

Even if future device advances eventually allow ChatGPT-size systems — and their guardrails — to run on edge devices, this tipping mechanism will survive. The CCDH study 40 sent 60 high-risk prompts to ChatGPT-4o (×20\times 20 repeats, N=1,200N=1{,}200) and found harmful content in 53% of responses, varying by domain (44% self-harm, 66% eating disorders, 50% substance abuse). Four qualitatively distinct features of these results map onto distinct structural properties of Eq. 2 (SI Table S2): (1) domain-dependent Δraw\Delta_{\rm raw} yields domain-dependent n∗n^{*}; (2) 𝐂\mathbf{C} vectors aligned toward 𝐃\mathbf{D} collapse n∗n^{*} to ≈0\approx\!0; (3) 𝐃\mathbf{D} tokens are self-reinforcing: each lowers n∗n^{*} further; (4) near-boundary prompts tip stochastically at finite TT. Though precise internal embeddings of ChatGPT-4o are not accessible for direct evaluation, four independent predictions from a single formula – applied to a system three orders of magnitude larger than the one on which it was quantitatively validated – constitute a non-trivial test.

Unlike static classification tools such as linear probes, which must be retrained per domain and per model, Eq. 2 is domain-portable and predicts dynamics — tipping delay, escalation, and control levers — while providing its own reliability indicator: wide bootstrap CIs and |Δ^raw|≈0|\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}|\approx 0 diagnose when a prompt sits near a basin boundary and the prediction should be treated as stochastic rather than deterministic. Even if multiple basins compete, there will always be a pair whose dot products are closest – and extending Eq. 2 to include 𝐃𝟏\bf{D}_{1}, 𝐃𝟐\bf{D}_{2} etc. is straightforward.

Methods

Model and generation.

All code is provided online. The 124M-parameter, 12-layer decoder-only architecture of the model used to generate the conversations in Figs. 1, 2 (GPT-241) places it squarely in the parameter range (100M–3B) of models currently deployed on mobile devices, sharing the same decoder-only transformer design as the Llama, Gemma, and Phi model families. SI Table S1 reports results for five additional decoder-only transformers (GPT-2-medium, Pythia-160m, Pythia-410m, OPT-125m, OPT-350m). SI Sec. 6 gives the n∗n^{*} derivation for a generic multilayer system. Dominant processing of concepts typically occurs within a few (e.g. final) layers and a few attention heads 33; 47, motivating the coarse-graining to an effective head.

Embedding extraction and basin construction.

All embeddings are extracted using the HuggingFace Transformers library 48. Hidden states at the penultimate transformer layer are mean-pooled across token positions; this layer is used because Eq. 2 replaces the final layer with an analytic attention expression (SI Sec. 3.9) 49; 42. Independent verification that Eq. 2 is coupled to genuine learned semantic geometry comes from evaluating it at different layers: first-layer embeddings, where the semantic distinction has not yet formed, yield incorrect predictions, whereas penultimate-layer embeddings produce correct ones (SI Sec. 14, Figs. S17, S19, S20). Basin centroids 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D} are means of NX=6N_{X}=6 phrase embeddings per category (e.g. 𝐁={‘Earth is round’,‘The Earth is a sphere’,…}{\bf B}=\{\text{`Earth is round'},\text{`The Earth is a sphere'},\ldots\}) and are held fixed across all models. These centroids are stable under larger phrase sets due to a centre-of-mass averaging effect. Full phrase lists are given in the SI. The coarse-graining from Eq. 1 is a restructuring of sums, with the approximation that each sentence’s projection onto the (𝐁,𝐃)({\bf B},{\bf D}) subspace is captured by its centroid 50; 51; 37; 52; 53.

Metrics.

The qualitative tipping direction is assessed from the sign of the raw dot-product difference Δraw≡𝐀⋅𝐃−𝐀⋅𝐁\Delta_{\rm raw}\equiv{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf D}-{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf B}, since these are the quantities the attention mechanism operates on (si​j=𝐪i⋅𝐤j/dks_{ij}={\bf q}_{i}\!\cdot\!{\bf k}_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}). The exact normalization lies between a raw-dot-product limit and a cosine-normalized limit, depending on the particular architecture’s layer normalization. LayerNorm periodically compresses but does not fix hidden-state norms, placing vectors on a fuzzy sphere whose radius fluctuates across layers (coefficient of variation 2–6% across architectures; SI Sec. 3.5) 54. Both the directional alignment and the residual norm asymmetry therefore enter the attention competition, which is why Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} is typically 1–2 orders of magnitude larger than Δcos≡cos⁡(𝐀,𝐃)−cos⁡(𝐀,𝐁)\Delta_{\cos}\equiv\cos({\bf A},{\bf D})-\cos({\bf A},{\bf B}) and why its sign is the more reliable predictor of tipping direction. Because the absolute scale of high-dimensional dot products is large (∼105\sim\!10^{5}–10610^{6} for d=768d=768), all six pairwise dot products for each prompt are divided by the largest among them for readability; the resulting scaled index is Δ^raw≡Δraw/max\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}\equiv\Delta_{\rm raw}/\max. The tipping-point estimate n∗n^{*} (Eq. 2) is evaluated in the unit-normalized (cosine) limit, where the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality guarantees that the denominator is negative and the Boltzmann competition between basins is well defined (SI Sec. 12.7).

Bootstrap and statistical assessment.

Bootstrap resampling (N=200N=200) of the six basin phrases gives 95% confidence intervals on Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw}, Δcos\Delta_{\cos}, and n∗n^{*}. Individual bootstrap CIs on Δ^raw\hat{\Delta}_{\rm raw} span zero for most model–prompt pairs because six basin phrases provide limited resampling power; the statistical evidence therefore resides in cross-model sign consistency (6/6 positive for both Flat Earth and Vaccines, binomial p=0.031p=0.031 per prompt). Models within each family share training corpora and are not fully independent, but all three independent groups (OpenAI, EleutherAI, Meta) agree on the tipping direction for both safety-critical prompts.

Dual-codebase robustness.

To check robustness, we verified that the geometric diagnostic 𝐀⋅𝐃>𝐀⋅𝐁{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf D}>{\bf A}\!\cdot\!{\bf B} is reproduced by an independently developed codebase (code supplied) that uses different basin phrases, a different model-loading class, and raw dot products rather than cosine similarities as its primary metric; details are given in the SI.

CCDH mapping.

The CCDH study 40 used multi-step conversations whose full transcripts are not publicly available; SI Table S2 therefore maps structural predictions of Eq. 2 to observed phenomenology rather than attempting direct quantitative evaluation. The logistic-map reduction (SI Secs. 8–9) predicts period-doubling oscillations (𝐁→𝐃→𝐁→𝐃​…{\bf B}\to{\bf D}\to{\bf B}\to{\bf D}\ldots) under high MLP gain or low temperature; we observe these patterns in all tested models and in the traces from ChatGPT-4o 40; 46.

Real-time deployment cost.

Practical basin centroids can be precomputed offline for each domain of concern and stored as a lightweight lookup table; updating Δraw\Delta_{\rm raw} requires only a running weighted sum over the context window. The per-token cost reduces to a small number of dot products against precomputed centroid vectors 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D}, an operation that scales as dd and is therefore negligible compared with the d2d^{2} cost of the forward pass itself. The dominant overhead is not computation but definition: specifying the centroid phrases that define 𝐁{\bf B} and 𝐃{\bf D} for each domain and cultural setting. This is a one-time annotation task analogous to defining classification labels, and can be updated independently of the model weights. In deployment, Eq. 2 therefore functions as a low-cost monitor that runs in parallel with generation, flagging when the predicted n∗n^{*} falls below a safety threshold without modifying the generation pipeline itself.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
